strengths: Timely and well-motivated work addressing the underexplored problem of in-generation watermarking for autoregressive (AR) visual generators, where naive adaptation of LLM watermarking fails due to VQ-VAE quantization discrepancies.
The proposed token-clustering approach is conceptually clear, elegant, and provides a viable training-free baseline that substantially improves robustness compared to naive token-level partitioning.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple modern AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B, GPT-L, and RAR-XL), benchmarking against traditional post-hoc methods (DWT-DCT-SVD, RivaGAN, TrustMark, SSL) and concurrent in-generation methods (IndexMark, WMAR).

Detailed ablation studies covering image fidelity (FID, CLIP scores), verification latency, cluster granularity, penalty hyperparameters, prefix sensitivity, and geometric transformations (with SyncSeal integration).
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is relatively moderate, as clustering embeddings to stabilize green/red set membership is an established concept in semantic LLM watermarking, and fine-tuning an encoder/classifier with data augmentation shares significant conceptual overlap with concurrent AR watermarking works (WMAR and IndexMark).

The training-free clustering method still exhibits noticeable drops in detection performance against common high-frequency or spatial disruptions (such as Gaussian blur and salt-and-pepper noise), necessitating the trained classifier to achieve competitive robustness.

The reliance on 'prefix tuning' (empirically selecting the best hash seed to suppress false positives caused by uniform visual regions) serves as a practical heuristic, but it highlights an inherent bias in visual token sequences that would benefit from a more fundamental mathematical or design formulation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely topic: while in-generation watermarking has been widely explored for diffusion models, watermarking autoregressive (AR) visual generators remains underexplored.

Provides a clear analysis of why direct adaptation of LLM token watermarking (KGW) fails in visual token spaces (quantization boundaries and encoding mismatches) and proposes an intuitive, well-motivated solution by clustering codebook embeddings.
Offers both an efficient training-free baseline and an optional lightweight token/cluster predictor that avoids modifying or degrading the generative model or the VAE decoder.

Extensive experimental evaluation across three AR architectures (LlamaGen GPT-B, GPT-L, RAR-XL) against relevant post-hoc and concurrent in-generation baselines (IndexMark, WMAR), demonstrating superior robustness against strong noise, color jitter, compression, and regeneration attacks while maintaining low verification runtime (~10–25 ms) and minimal FID degradation.
Thorough ablation analysis covering cluster count k, watermark bias delta, green ratio gamma, hash prefix sensitivity, and cluster initialization.
weaknesses: Inherently vulnerable to geometric transformations (cropping, rotation, translation) due to raster-scan decoding order; mitigating this requires external pre-synchronization modules such as SyncSeal.

The prefix-tuning step reveals an underlying sensitivity to spatial autocorrelation and large uniform image regions, where repetitive visual token bigrams cause false positive inflation under unfortunate hash seeds.

The proposed method is strictly formulated as a zero-bit detection scheme (presence vs. absence via p-value), lacking exploration or demonstration of multi-bit payload embedding for message extraction or fine-grained attribution.
The clustering methodology is tightly coupled to discrete VQ-VAE codebooks and does not easily extend to modern continuous-token visual autoregressive models (e.g., FLUID).

strengths: Timely and well-motivated topic: While in-generation watermarking has been extensively studied for diffusion models, watermarking discrete autoregressive (AR) image generation models remains relatively underexplored despite their growing prominence (e.g., LlamaGen, RAR).

Clear insight and sound methodology: The paper accurately identifies that naive KGW watermarking fails due to codebook quantization sensitivity under perturbations. Grouping codebook vectors via k-means clustering to construct cluster-level green/red sets is an intuitive, elegant, and largely training-free solution to this issue.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors conduct extensive experiments across multiple models and resolutions (LlamaGen GPT-B 256, GPT-L 384, and RAR-XL 256), benchmark against multiple classical post-hoc methods and recent concurrent in-generation AR watermarking techniques (IndexMark, WMAR), and generate millions of images for rigorous statistical evaluations (AUC, TPR@FPR=1%, FID, CLIP score).

Practical verification efficiency: Unlike diffusion-based watermarks that require expensive iterative latent inversion, the proposed watermark verification is extremely fast (~10–25 ms per image), matching lightweight post-hoc methods.

Dual operating regimes: The paper provides both a completely training-free approach and an optional lightweight encoder fine-tuning scheme (cluster/token classifier) that significantly boosts robustness against severe corruptions (e.g., salt-and-pepper noise, heavy blur).
weaknesses: Inherent vulnerability to geometric distortions: Like many token-level spatial watermarks, the method is vulnerable to cropping, rotation, and translation out-of-the-box. While the supplementary material demonstrates that an external synchronization module (SyncSeal) can mitigate this, the standalone method remains sensitive to spatial alignment.

Dependence on empirical prefix tuning: The detection performance and false positive rates show considerable variance across different hash seeds/prefixes due to common repetitive background tokens (e.g., uniform flat patches). While the authors candidly analyze this in Section 4.3 and Appendix D, requiring pre-deployment prefix filtering is a notable limitation that warrants a more principled algorithmic solution.

Quality vs. robustness trade-off for low cluster counts: High robustness in the training-free setting pushes the method toward lower cluster counts ($k \le 32$), which causes observable visual artifacts and noticeable FID degradation, limiting the effective operational envelope to around $k=64$ unless paired with the trained classifier.

strengths: Addresses an important and emerging problem: While in-generation watermarking has been extensively studied for latent diffusion models, watermarking autoregressive (AR) visual generators has remained largely underexplored.

Provides a clear and insightful analysis of why naive token-level red-green watermarking fails in AR image models—namely, the fragility of discrete VQ-VAE token reconstruction under minor perturbations and quantization boundaries.

Proposes a well-motivated two-tier solution: an effective training-free codebook clustering method that significantly improves resilience, along with a perturbation-trained Cluster Classifier (+CC) that handles severe degradations (e.g., salt-and-pepper noise, blur).

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The paper conducts massive experiments (generating over 4.7 million images) across multiple architectures (LlamaGen GPT-B/L, RAR-XL), various perturbation types, and regeneration attacks (SD1.5, FLUX.1, SD2.1).

Detailed ablation studies analyzing key hyperparameters (number of clusters k, logit bias delta, green token ratio gamma, hash prefix sensitivity) and their corresponding impact on both detection performance (TPR@1%FPR, AUC) and visual quality (FID).
Highlights an important practical advantage: Watermark verification operates in milliseconds, avoiding the heavy computational inversion costs typical of diffusion-based in-generation watermarks.
weaknesses: Methodological selection of the hash prefix: The authors observe noticeable variance across different hash prefixes kappa and report results using the best prefix identified across all perturbations. In a real-world setting, finding the optimal prefix would require an explicit held-out validation protocol to prevent over-optimistic evaluation.

Lack of robustness against spatial/geometric transformations: Like many patch/token-level watermarking schemes, the method is inherently susceptible to geometric operations such as cropping, rotation, and scaling due to the disruption of raster-order alignment and patch grids.

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: The core formulation heavily builds upon Kirchenbauer et al.'s LLM watermarking and semantic clustering ideas previously explored in NLP watermarking, although adapting and stabilizing it for visual discrete tokenizers is technically sound.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: While in-generation watermarking has been extensively studied for latent diffusion models, watermarking for discrete autoregressive (AR) image generators remains largely underexplored despite the growing prominence of visual AR models.

Clear insight and sound methodology: The paper clearly identifies why directly porting LLM red-green watermarks fails for images (sensitivity of VQ-VAE codebook quantization to subtle pixel shifts) and provides an elegant, well-principled solution by operating at the cluster level.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors validate their approaches across multiple models (LlamaGen GPT-B, GPT-L, and RAR-XL), standard benchmarks (ImageNet 50k FID), a wide range of perturbations (blur, compression, noise, color jitter, regeneration attacks), and detailed ablation studies.

Verification efficiency: The paper demonstrates that AR token watermarking verification is orders of magnitude faster (10-25 ms) than inversion-based watermarking schemes for diffusion models (e.g., Tree-Ring), while outperforming post-hoc baselines and concurrent AR watermarking techniques.
weaknesses: Vulnerability to geometric transformations: Because the watermarking process relies strictly on a fixed raster scan order and grid alignment with the VQ-VAE patches, common geometric attacks (e.g., cropping, rotation, scaling) fundamentally disrupt token synchronization. While acknowledged in Section 6, empirical quantification or discussion of potential mitigation strategies (e.g., spatial realignment or local synchronization) is lacking.

Generalization of the Cluster Classifier to unseen perturbations: The Cluster Classifier is finetuned using perturbation data augmentations (Table 6) that closely mirror the evaluation suite (Gaussian noise, JPEG, blur, salt & pepper). An evaluation under unseen/out-of-distribution perturbations would help clarify how much of the performance gain is due to general cluster robustness versus memorization of specific corruption types.

Prefix selection protocol: The 'prefix tuning' step optimizes the hash salt $\kappa$ based on robustness evaluations. While the appendix shows that mean performance across prefixes remains strong (Tables 8 and 9), cherry-picking the best prefix across evaluated perturbations borders on optimistic evaluation unless evaluated strictly on a disjoint validation split.

Minor notation and typesetting inconsistencies: In the caption of Table 1, $\lambda = 0.25$ is written instead of $\gamma = 0.25$. In Algorithm 1 line 2, `C[q_{-1}]` should be `C[q_{i-1}]`, and line 22 refers to `x_{1:n}` instead of generated tokens.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: While in-generation watermarking has been extensively explored for latent diffusion models, watermarking autoregressive (AR) discrete-token image generators remains underexplored.

The core insight is clear and sound: The paper accurately identifies that naive token-level red-green watermarking fails because VQ-VAE quantization is brittle under perturbations, and proposes visual token clustering and cluster-level red/green partitioning to mitigate this issue.

Provides both a lightweight, training-free approach (codebook k-means clustering) and an enhanced learning-based approach (adversarially finetuning the encoder as a Cluster Classifier), giving practical flexibility.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Validated across multiple AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B, GPT-L, and RAR-XL) under a wide range of realistic image perturbations, including diffusion- and autoencoder-based regeneration attacks, consistently outperforming post-hoc baselines and naive watermarking.
Demonstrates fast verification runtime (10–25 ms per image), highlighting a major efficiency advantage over diffusion-inversion watermarking methods (e.g., Tree-Ring).
weaknesses: Vulnerability to geometric transformations: As acknowledged in the conclusion, token-level watermarking is fundamentally susceptible to spatial misalignments caused by geometric transforms (such as cropping, rotation, or scaling). While common among patch-based generative watermarks, this remains a practical vulnerability.

Methodology behind Prefix Tuning: The paper observes substantial variance across hash prefixes (kappa) and selects the best prefix based on average TPR across the test perturbations. It is not entirely clear whether this constitutes test-set leakage or how well a prefix tuned on synthetic perturbations generalizes to unseen real-world distortions.

Training overhead of the Cluster Classifier: The best-performing variant (+CC) requires finetuning an encoder over 100k generated images with a specific perturbation schedule, which adds training complexity and makes the approach dependent on the chosen set of training augmentations.

Quality-robustness trade-off at lower cluster counts: While k=64 preserves FID relatively well, smaller cluster counts (k <= 32) cause noticeable degradation in image fidelity (higher FID scores and visual artifacts), limiting how aggressively one can coarsen the clusters to gain robustness.
